title: Designing a Live-and-Work House 2027: Frontage, Access, Storage
desc: Laying out a house combining home and business: sales frontage, separate access to the living area, storage, fire separation under the Fire Law, change of use.
summary: Experience designing a house for both living and business: separating circulation, planning storage, the frontage, and the mandatory fire protection requirements under the 2024 Law on Fire Prevention, Fighting and Rescue.
body: p

A townhouse for both living and trading is a very common model. Good design makes business convenient while the family still lives privately and safely. The key point is to separate the living and business areas, especially in access and fire protection.
h2
1. Decide the type of business from the start
p
The layout, storage, ventilation and fire protection requirements depend on what you sell. Under Article 21 of the 2024 Law on Fire Prevention, Fighting and Rescue:
ul

Every house combined with production or business must have prohibition signs, warning signs and directional signs as prescribed; the area for goods with a fire or explosion risk must have separation or fire-resistant measures from the living area.

If you trade in goods dangerous in fire or explosion (gas, petrol, chemicals and so on): no sleeping places in the business area; suitable fire alarms, ventilation and gas leak detection equipment; and the business area must be fire-separated from the escape routes of the living area.
p
For details of fire protection conditions, see Houses combined with business: fire prevention and fighting conditions.
h2
2. Frontage and ground floor
ul
Give priority on the ground floor to openness, wide doors and few columns blocking sight lines; a ceiling high enough to fit signs, lights and shelves.

Canopies, awnings and signboards must not project beyond the permitted extent. Under QCVN 01:2026 (in force from 1 January 2027), projecting architectural details must not obstruct traffic, pedestrians on the pavement, trees, infrastructure and fire engines (Section 2.5.7); advertising boards must follow the regulations on outdoor advertising (Section 2.5.10).
Leave customer parking space within the premises if possible, avoiding encroaching on the pavement.
h2
3. A separate entrance for the living area
p

It is advisable to provide an entrance and stairs to the living area that do not pass through the shop counter or storage. Common solutions: a side or rear door, or a small lobby beside the shop leading straight to the stairs. Benefits:
ul
The family can come and go when the shop is closed without opening the roller shutter.
If a fire breaks out in the business area, people upstairs still have an escape route - consistent with the requirement for fire separation from the living area's escape route.

A house must provide and maintain escape routes, emergency exits or passages ensuring escape (Point b, Clause 2, Article 20). So avoid sealing balconies and windows with iron frames that have no opening escape hatch.
h2
4. Storage
ul
Put storage where goods are easy to receive (at the rear, near the side door), not blocking walkways and stairs.
Do not keep flammable goods near the kitchen, ancestral altar or sockets; provide separate electricity for the business area with protective devices.
Heavy storage on a floor slab needs the engineer to calculate the load - do not turn a bedroom into a heavy-goods store on your own.
h2
5. Converting a home to business use
p

When changing the use of part or all of a single-family house together with repair or renovation, the design and construction must comply with regulations and standards suited to the new use (Clause 5, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). Note: the permit exemption for internal repair applies only when there is no change of use purpose or function (Point h, Clause 2, Article 43 of the Construction Law 2025), so for a renovation that changes use, check the procedure carefully before starting.
h2
6. Checklist
ol
Is the type of goods sold fire- or explosion-hazardous?
Does the living area have its own entrance and stairs or is it fire-separated from the business area?
Are suitable signs, extinguishers and fire alarms in place?
Do the canopy and signboard encroach on the pavement?
Has the goods-storing floor been calculated for load?
p

note

This article is for reference; every work needs to be surveyed and designed by a qualified person. The 2024 Law on Fire Prevention, Fighting and Rescue is partly expired; QCVN 01:2026/BXD takes effect on 1 January 2027. Ask the police fire authority about fire protection and the commune- or ward-level People's Committee about construction procedures where the house is located.
